title: Last Straws: John Chaffe, Bris Jones, Bill Lee, Frank De La Houssaye, Bob Ice Interview, 1960-04-18

blocks.x: You know, it'd be deep. Unprint. Okay. Okay, we're ready. Well, it's the night before Christmas. You got it going? Okay, we're recording this at 2607 Jefferson Avenue. Right. And today is April what? 18th. 1960, and what's your name?
John Chass.

Mm-hmm. And my name's Dick Allen. We're going to put this in the archive, too. So I don't have everybody's name on when the secretary translates. Let's see, John, personal questions first. When were you born and where?
1938, here in the city.
And your exact date of birth?
March 29th.
Quite recent. Relatively, yeah. You all just had a birthday. Do your family play music?
No, no one in the family does. Mm-hmm. At least in the immediate family.

And we've got some notes here on the Banjo Bombs records that you started out on piano at eight? That's about right. Mm-hmm. And when you were 10, you were playing clarinet in the grammar school band. No, that's a mistake.

Mm-hmm. That was Malcolm Janay that they had referred to there and then got it mixed up. Now, the next thing I started playing was guitar. And then from guitar to you being lazy guitarist and then to banjo. And bass came in there about 1951. What kind of a bass? Bass horn, susaphone, tuba. Mm-hmm.
And you continued on that very long?
I played for about six years.
When did you take banjo about the first time?
About the same time that I began bass.
Did you have any lessons when you started?
No, I, well, to a certain degree. The only real teacher I ever had was Lawrence Marrero.
And what did he teach you?
Mostly jazz style. And just rudiments, jazz, banjo.
Did he teach you many different rhythms? He specialized in one particular type of rhythm.
Mostly one particular type of rhythm, of course, is the one that Lewis has known so well for, that straightforward beat. But I think he's responsible for any beat that I have today, really.
When did you start playing with bands?

Well, I think the first attempt was the banjo bums, which was, well, my first attempt actually was with Malcolm Janay. We just had a duet there for about two or three years during high school. And then the banjo bums was organized in 1955. And the recording was made in 1956.
And who was in it, who was in the banjo bums other than you and Janay?
Dr. Sushant and Sherry Manjapain. Sushant on? Guitar. Manjapain on bass.
Just like the record, in other words. Yes. And what kind of jobs did you play with the banjo bums?

Well, the banjo bums was almost primarily a recording group. We got it together as just a fun string group, and then we decided to record, and we did record. And since then, of course, our jobs have been very limited because of the limited range of a group like this. And lately, our only thing has been getting together once a year to play down on Royal Street during the Spring Fiesta. But during the earlier days, Janay and I made a couple of trips to Houston to play in the Shamrock Hotel.
Okay, let's see. We were talking about the Shamrock. You played at the Shamrock Hotel? Yeah. Wow. You played at the Shamrock, huh? With the banjo bums? Right. How long were you there?
Oh, we were just there one night for two successive years.
And when did the last straws get formed?
Let's see. That was about 1957. Yeah, it was October of 1957.
Did you play with any other bands besides the last straw?
Oh, I played a couple nights with Sherrod Manjapan's group.
Up at the jazz club, too.
Well, I played a great year up at the jazz club. Yeah, but nothing, you know, on a permanent basis or anything like that. Our job basis. With the exception of Manjapan's group.
That's a nice way to record. What sort of style were you aiming at with the last straws when you first started?

Well, when we first started, we started Riverboat because we didn't have anything with a piano and bass and drums and bandroom. What was that? Oh, it was Bob McIntyre on drums and Bob Ice on bass and Frank Tallahoussi on piano and myself on banjo.
And what kind of bass was that? What was that?

That was strictly a homemade two-string bass. The one he played until recently, then? Yes, the one he played up until about two months ago. And what did you add into the band? Well, the first thing we added was a cornet. Joe Lide, who was an Englishman who was over here. And before Joe left, we had added Briss Jones, the present clarinetist. And then Joe left us, and we picked up Manuel Zanko, the well-known moose, who played cornet for us. And then Bill Lee came in with his soprano sax clarinet.
Archie?
Archie, yes. And now that Archie is rather in and out with us, we have Nick Agniotti, who plays trombone with us now.
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's Archie Rogers. Right. Now, let's see. As the band grew, what style were you aiming for then?
Older and older. The style is as archaic as possible, and still, in a sense.
Who are your favorite musicians?

Well, I don't really single them out, because I like the sound of a whole band rather than any one musician together. And I suppose if I had to pick any real favorites, of course, in the single musician field, I'd pick Louis Armstrong before 1930, and King Oliver and George Lewis and Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds both.
Any banjo players? That's what I would like.

Well, I like St. Cyr's style a great deal. Of course, he's a six-string man. And I really like Blanche Murrow's style. It was very, very straight, but it certainly was tremendous in adding to the beat because the rest of the rhythm section worked the same way. I think it's very important to have a rhythm section for everybody working together.
What about whole band?

Concentrate the same type of beat. As far as the whole band's concerned, I think that Jelly Roll Martin's Red Hot Peppers is the finest band that I had ever heard. However, there are several other bands which I have heard that I like very much, named with the New Orleans Feet Warmers, I believe, and the old Armstrong Hot 7, 1925-26 Hot 7.
Well, I think that just about covers your background. Why don't we see if we can get next. What about Chris up here? Chris, can you come over and do a little talking?
Yeah, well, I'll do a little talking.
Yeah.
Let's see. I don't say anything bad about James.

Yeah. Swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, nothing but the truth shall help you forward. This is going in the jazz archive. Going in the jazz archives. Yeah, and also we want to get a little background, just enough for the album notes, you see. Like, when you were born and where?
Well, that's what you want? Well, Bogalusa, 1926. Bogalusa, Louisiana.
And what, exactly what day?
July 12th.
And what's your full name?
Malcolm Brister Jones.
They just called you Briss, huh?
That's right. Not Malcolm, I hope.
Do you remember Snoozer Quinn over there?

I heard quite a bit about him. I didn't know him. He died when I was first getting interested in playing. And everyone was talking about Snooze. I believe he played with White when it was something like that.
Yeah, he did.
See, he was great.
He made a few records, you ought to hear.
Yeah, he died over here at the hospital, I believe, a few years back.
And did they have any jazz bands over there when you were growing up?

No, I never even thought of jazz whatsoever. Until, well, I guess my first interest was in singing. And I was on a ship and Bill Lee came on the ship. And he had a clarinet. So I used to sing and he would play. And finally we decided I should get a clarinet and we'd play together. That's the way I made my entry into the study of music.
Were you reading?
Yes.
You read music then? Right. Did you have any teacher other than Bill?
Irving Fazol. I studied with him for a few months in the summer of 48, not long before he died. Probably one of Faz's few students that he ever had, actually, you know, as far as studio stuff.
Mm-hmm. When did you start playing with bands?

Well, I played a little bit with bands in Boga Loosa, reading bands. And then when I was in the Army, I played with the band, naturally, you know, the dance band. And played around with guys a little bit. But actually, I didn't really start playing with Dixieland until Moose called. I go to school, you know, a GI school, Educational Gateways. And Moose called about a clarinet player. So I met Moose when I started playing with, you know, Moose and Norman and Gene. Norman who? Duripo. Gene Fulon. We got together at the house, you know, every week. You got your back? Just fun. Yeah. And so since Norman and Gene were members of the jazz club, we were invited to play up there. So that's where John heard us and heard me. And so I started with the straw. That's the way I first got into really playing.

Excuse me a second. Harry, can you watch the level? What? The level on the machine. So we don't know where it going. Because I want to get a little closer into the mic if we can here. Let's see. And you played saxophone or clarinet?
Yeah, sax. Sax with a dance band, yes. What sax? Well, tenor and alto. I even played baritone. When I was in the army, I played baritone for quite a while.
Mm-hmm. I see. When did you start playing with the straws?

Well, that was in, let's see, September 1958. It was September 22nd that we played at the jazz club. The band would call ourselves the Tin Roofers. Nothing professional, just house fun, you know, house parties and so forth. And so John heard us and the following week I made a rehearsal with the straws, Sunday after that. And that's when I've been playing with the straws since around the first of October, 1958.
See? Mm-hmm. Who are some of your favorite musicians?

What are some of my favorites? Well, I'll tell you, I liked some of the later guys. Fuzzola, naturally. I liked him very much. And, well, I listened to all of it. I mean, I like all styles of music as far as that. All the different types, modern jazz, you know, Dixieland, old jazz. It all was interesting. As a matter of fact, I like to kind of change up and listen to different, you know, different types at different times. And, naturally, Pete Fountain, I listen to him a lot.
Did any particular bands you like as a group?

Well, my first interest was Harry James. Mm-hmm. First band that I had interest in, and the trumpet and so forth. I guess if I'd had a choice and I'd have thought about it, I would have taken trumpet.
Well, I think that's good enough. We'll call on somebody. Okay. Bill Lee. Can you talk a minute? Let's see. What's your name first? Bill Lee.
Hey, no, I didn't like 10 years.

Okay, that's enough. And when were you born and where? Memphis, Tennessee. December the 26th, 1926. December the 19th, 1926. Mm-hmm. And did you have any musicians in your family? No. Oh, Bress, I wanted to ask you. Do you have any musicians in your family? No, no. Bress says he doesn't have any musicians in his family. And you don't. That explains it.
That explains it. That explains it. That explains it. That explains it. That explains it.

Mm-hmm. And so, how did you get interested in music? Well, I've always liked jazz. The first time I heard it, and I think Fazola was about the first one I heard back in the late 30s, I guess. With, well, actually he was back in New Orleans the first time I heard him, but before that, you know, he was with Bob Crosby. But I was always crazy about his style from the first. In fact, that's the reason I took clarinet. Yeah. Did you know him well? No, I only knew him through Bress, actually. Bress took lessons from him. Yeah. Who's it? Well, uh, how long was it before you took up music after the...
and to get interested? By what year would you say?
1940 or 41, I guess. It's been kind of hit and miss ever since.
Did you have a teacher then?
Well, I went to, I was in a school band in Woodville, Mississippi, for a while. The different schools that I attended, that's about all, actually.
You really got around.
You lived in a lot of places. Oh, well, I was born in Memphis, but my home has always been Woodville, Mississippi. I mean, that was my hometown until I went to a couple other schools.

I've been through there. I was selling fish there, I noticed, last weekend. I was at, right on the square. I was looking for a guitar player from there, Scott Dunbar. Oh? Yeah, he's a real good guitar player. He's made some records. When were you there? A couple of weeks ago, I was on my way to Natchez.
Well, I was in Natchez two weeks ago. In fact, I went to Woodville the same weekend, I bet you. Were you there on a Sunday?

I was there, I guess, on a Saturday, I think I got there. Oh, no. Went on up to Natchez. I just missed you. That's funny. Did you hear any bands around there that were playing any jazz when you were growing up?
No. No, not around my part of the country. Not at all. What did they play? How's that?
What did they play up there? What kind of music?
Well, you had a band on Saturday nights and such on the weekends, but it wasn't necessarily jazz. In fact, it never was jazz. Just regular pop.
Hillbilly song?
No. No, I never recall any hillbilly from that part of the country.
Did you play with dance bands then?

No, I didn't. I never played in Woodville. Well, yeah, I did. I had a little band there myself, but otherwise I never played with anybody else there. But I have played with hillbilly bands, and that was mostly over around Bristol's country. Incidentally, around Bogalusa. And, of course, down here.
When did you start playing jazz? I've been trying ever since I've... Ever since you started. But, I mean, when did you first play with a jazz band?
Well, I had a little group of my own about eight years ago, I guess. Roughly eight years ago. And we called ourselves jazz players. And then the last straws, I guess that's about all. That's it.
Now, how long have you been with the straws?
Hey, fellas, how long have I been playing with y'all?
You haven't started playing with us yet?
Ah, shut up. Two years? I would say since the spring of 59.
Since the spring of 59. No.
Well, I started out in November. Oh, well, it's been about a year then. About a year, yeah.
About a year. I see. What instruments do you play?
I try to play the sax and the clarinet.
And you specialize in now and soprano.
Yeah. Boss Toss decided I shouldn't specialize in soprano. I see.
Well, I've heard you play alto with the band, too, and clarinet.
Who are some of your favorites? Other than Fazella, you mentioned him. Oh, let's see. Well, I like quite a few around town. Bill Boudreau, I think his name is. Does he play with Mike Lawler?
Is that the fellow?
That's the one. Yeah. And quite a few. Tony Costa, do you remember him?
Yeah, I know him. Mm-hmm.
Others, of course, out of town. Matty Matlock, for instance. Of course, Eddie Miller, he's always a favorite. Mm-hmm. Shh.

Well, let's see. We're trying to jam everybody in at once. Let's see who we can get next. We aren't likely to get. Del? Del, come on over. I think we've got enough for the album. I know. Okay. First thing I need to know is your name.
Frank Delahousa. Mm-hmm.

And when were you born and where? Born in January the 8th, 1933, New Orleans. Mm-hmm. Do you have any musicians in your family? No. You're the black sheep? Black sheep. All right. When did you start getting interested in music?

Well, they had an old piano at home that they used to lock up, but I used to get the key and open it and bang on it. And that's how I started when I was about 10 years old. And I've just been banging around on the piano ever since then.
Any other instruments you play? Mm-hmm.
No.
Did you have a teacher on the piano?

No, I never did. Can you read? Can't read, no. I used to go down to the quad and watch Archibald play the piano. Mm-hmm. And that's actually how I really learned how to play, watching him when I was about, oh, freshman in college. And then about a year, oh, about six months after I was in the college, four of us in the K fraternity, myself, had a little Dixieland band at that time. We played for about two years together under the name of the Audubon Street Four Plus One. And then eventually that broke up, and I wasn't associated with another group until I started playing with the Last Straws, and I was with them when they originated. And then October of the 57th.
Who was in the other band, the Audubon Street?

That was, we had Stanley Barron on bass, Hughes Drums was on the drums, I was on piano, Bob Wolf was on banjo, and Jim Allen was on sax. And we played, we tried to play at Dixieland style with those instruments. We played together over at Tulane and various parties around there for about two years.
Did the other fellas continue on?
No, none of them did. As a matter of fact, I don't believe any of them were playing at all now. Got married, moved out of town most of them.
Have you played with any other bands? Mm-hmm. Who are some of your favorites? Let's see, we ought to get that down.

On what instruments? Well, on piano first. George Shearing is my favorite. Quite odd here. This type of music. But I really do like George Shearing rather. And I used to like, well I still do like some of the works. Fats Waller, Oscar Peterson and some of those guys.
Your style certainly doesn't sound like those fellas.

No, my style is strictly off of this fella in the quarter Archibald. I can't control my left hand and neither can he. The only way I can move it around would be to do it in an octave fashion. I can't manipulate it. Well, I'm not very dexterous, I guess you would say, with my left hand. I just have to chord.
What style do you play with the band when you're playing in the ensemble? What do you aim for?

Well, I just try to chord it the best I can. It's strictly chord music is what I'm doing. In the jazz it's strictly a swing. I mean it's truly not a swing, but I'm right on the beat all of the time with my left hand. I don't know what you'd call it. I see. Well, you're really... Strictly a native piano.
Yeah.
Well, that's... No, nothing about... It seems to fit in with the band, you know.
I mean that's what you're doing is helping the other guys along, giving them that nice harmony.
It's strictly a beat that is just in us, I guess.
I'm not now, nor have I ever been affiliated with.
Alright. What's your name? Robert Ice. And when were you born and where? 1931. In Fairmont, West Virginia. And your full name? Robert Stevens Ice. And your full date of birth?
January 1, 1931. January 3, 1931.
You have any family background of music?
Well, none other than my father being a... Playing the piano and also singing. Still doing quite a bit of singing.
Professional?
No, no. He sings with weddings. He sings in the church choir. Solo work and so forth. All the time. Still doing... But other than that, only an interest of my own.
When did you start in music yourself?

Well, I guess I've always had an interest in it. I've always liked dancing and... I tried the piano for about six months and... Actually was more interested in playing... Baseball. And so... As the usual American boy, I was out playing ball rather than practicing. How long was that? Oh, that was fifth or sixth grade, I guess. Later on then, of course, I... Did some vocal work with... Quartet work at school, college, high school also. And... And I got interested in the... While I was in college, I got interested in playing bass. Of course, I didn't have the funds to purchase a bass at the time, so I... Decided I'd build my own. Strictly as an experiment. But as it turned out, it was very, very interesting, very much fun.
And... What was the deal on that? When did you start on this space, this homemade bass?
Oh, it was the summer of... 51.
And who'd you play with?
Just a small group that we had at the fraternity house and... At school.
Where was this?
West Virginia University. We played... Oh, I guess you'd say... Along the progressive line. More than... Anything else.
When did you come to New Orleans?
Been to New Orleans about five years now. Thanksgiving in... 55. Right after I got out of the service.
You came down here to go to school?
No, I came down to visit. And... Gee, that... I was gonna stay about a week. That was four years ago. I'm still there. I'm still there. The man who came to dinner.
I was sleepy. I was about a week. Did you play with any bands when you first came down here?

No. Actually, the last straws, I would say, was the first... Organized group that... In New Orleans that I ever played with. We got together one Sunday afternoon just to have a little... Jam session and... Had a good little fun out of it. So we continued playing a couple of other times. And eventually... Some people became very interested in hearing his play. Or having his play for a small party. And from there we progressed to where we presently are.
Well, tell me a little bit about this Vienna trip. How did that come about?

Well, our trip to Vienna was primarily... A result of... Harry Sushant's... Interest in the group. Some people from New Orleans were interested... Of course, in having a Dixieland group at the festival. More or less as a counter... Effect against the... Communist... Interests. And they realized, of course, that Dixieland in Europe is... Or let's say jazz in Europe is a terrific attraction. And they wanted something that was truly New Orleans. And young at the same time. A youthful group that would fit in with the youth festival. But anyway... Harry recommended us to the people that were interested in sending the group. Thought that we would be a very logical choice. Of course, we were very flattered to be considered such by Mr. Sushant. Since he seems to be quite an authority on old-time jazz.
They treated you nice in Vienna, those communist times.

Well, they didn't particularly like us being there. No, they resented our... They resented our being there... Because they knew that we were not there in their interests. But... More in the interest of a true picture of America.
What about housing and food when you were there? Did they give you good housing?
Well, the housing was... That's a... It's kind of like y'all's housing, actually. To use the word loosely. Yeah. No, we stayed in barracks, actually. It was a large hall. Something like a... stuff

Stalag 17, that's Stalag 18 we call it. The food? The food was, well if you can prepare a meal for 9 cents a meal, 27 cents a day let's say, which was what we were actually allotted, I'd say you're doing pretty well. They tried but of course we were accustomed to food that was a little better prepared and they did, of course the Austrian catering service did prepare the food and there were a lot of complaints about it because it was undercooked and so forth. As it turned out I think everyone got a chance to get outside the festival because of the food as bad as it was in the festival we all got a chance to get out and try the Viennese menu which of course food in Vienna itself is fabulous, really delicious.
So how did the people receive you in Vienna? What did they think of you?

Generally speaking we made a wonderful hit because they were interested in jazz as I mentioned earlier. They were interested in New Orleans style and they felt that we represented New Orleans. All we had to do was mention the name New Orleans, New Orleans Jazz and resulted in a lot of autograph signing and so forth which we were definitely not accustomed to.
Did you play any place other than the festival?
Yeah we played outside the festival in a nightclub called Fatty's Saloon. We played there every night during the time we were in Vienna. stuff

segments.title: Session opening and John Chaffe's birth and family
segments.summary: Allen opens the recording at 2607 Jefferson Avenue on 18 April 1960 and asks Chaffe his birth date and whether his family plays music.

segments.title: Chaffe's instruments and lessons with Lawrence Marrero
segments.summary: Chaffe corrects the record on his start: piano, guitar, banjo, bass horn from about 1951. His only real teacher was Lawrence Marrero, who taught him jazz banjo style and a straightforward beat.

segments.title: The Banjo Bums and the Shamrock Hotel
segments.summary: Chaffe describes a duet with Malcolm Janay, then the Banjo Bums (1955, recorded 1956), mostly a recording group, with Royal Street gigs and two nights at the Houston Shamrock.

segments.title: Forming the Last Straws and its lineup
segments.summary: The Last Straws formed in October 1957 with Bob McIntyre, Bob Ice, Frank De La Houssaye and Chaffe. Later came Joe Lide, Bris Jones, Manuel Zanko, Bill Lee and Nick Agniotti, aiming for an archaic style.

segments.title: Chaffe's favorite musicians, banjoists and bands
segments.summary: Chaffe favors the whole-band sound. He names Armstrong, King Oliver, George Lewis, the Dodds, St. Cyr and Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers.

segments.title: Bris Jones: birth and name
segments.summary: Allen brings up Jones, who says he was born in Bogalusa, Louisiana, on July 12, 1926, full name Malcolm Brister Jones.

segments.title: Jones's start on clarinet and lessons with Fazola
segments.summary: After a chat about Snoozer Quinn, Jones says he wasn't into jazz at first. He met Bill Lee on a ship and took up clarinet to play with him, and studied with Irving Fazola in summer 1948.

segments.title: Jones's bands: Army, the Tin Roofers and joining the Straws
segments.summary: Jones played in reading and Army dance bands, then Dixieland with Moose, Norman and Gene as the Tin Roofers. John heard them at the jazz club and Jones joined the Straws in October 1958.

segments.title: Jones's favorite musicians and bands
segments.summary: Jones likes Fazola, Pete Fountain and all styles, and says Harry James's band was his first interest.

segments.title: Bill Lee: birth, family, Fazola and early music
segments.summary: Lee was born in Memphis in December 1926 and has no musicians in the family. Fazola's style is why he took clarinet, around 1940-41. He played in a school band in Woodville, Mississippi.

segments.title: Music around Woodville and Lee's first jazz group
segments.summary: After talk of Natchez and Woodville, Lee says there was no jazz there, only pop. He played hillbilly bands and led his own small jazz group about eight years earlier.

segments.title: Lee joins the Last Straws; instruments and favorites
segments.summary: Lee has played with the Straws roughly a year, since late 1959. He plays sax and clarinet, and likes Bill Boudreau, Tony Costa, Matty Matlock and Eddie Miller.

segments.title: De La Houssaye: learning piano and the Audubon Street Four Plus One
segments.summary: Frank De La Houssaye, born 1933, taught himself piano and learned watching Archibald. He played in a college Dixieland band, the Audubon Street Four Plus One, before the Last Straws.

segments.title: De La Houssaye's favorite pianists and his style
segments.summary: He favors George Shearing, Fats Waller and Oscar Peterson, but his own style comes from Archibald. He plays chords on the beat because his left hand is limited.

segments.title: Bob Ice: birth, family and early music
segments.summary: Bob Ice was born in Fairmont, West Virginia, in 1931. His father played piano and sang. Ice tried piano, then sang in quartets and built his own bass.

segments.title: Homemade bass, West Virginia University and coming to New Orleans
segments.summary: Ice built a bass in summer 1951 and played with a fraternity group at West Virginia University. He came to New Orleans in 1955, and the Last Straws was his first organized group there.

segments.title: How the Vienna festival trip came about
segments.summary: Harry Souchon recommended the Straws as a youthful New Orleans group for the Vienna youth festival, as a counter to Communist influence. The festival hosts resented them being there.

segments.title: Housing, food and reception in Vienna
segments.summary: The band stayed in barracks and ate poor festival food on a tiny allowance. They were a hit with audiences and played nightly at Fatty's Saloon.
